questions.question: What are generics in Java, what problem do they solve, and what does type erasure cost you?
questions.title: Java Generics — What They Solve, What They Give You, What Type Erasure Costs
questions.direct_answer: **Generics** let you parameterize classes, interfaces, and methods with a **type variable** (e.g., `List<T>`) so the compiler can enforce type safety and remove casts. **Before generics (Java 4 and earlier)**, collections stored `Object` — errors showed up at runtime as `ClassCastException`, often far from the real bug. **Generics moved the check to compile time** and eliminated manual casts. **The cost**: Java uses **type erasure** for backward compatibility — `T` is erased to `Object` (or its bound) in bytecode, so you can't do `new T()`, `new T[]`, or `instanceof List<String>` at runtime. You get compile-time safety for free; the runtime remembers nothing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can explain the pre-generics pain, the compile-time benefits, and understands that erasure is the cost of backward compatibility
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming generics 'make code run faster' (they don't — they're compile-time only). Thinking `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are different classes at runtime. Not knowing that JDK 5 preserved backward compatibility via erasure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that C# chose reified generics with backward-incompatible runtime changes while Java chose erasure for backward compatibility. Discuss how diamond operator (Java 7) reduced verbosity further, and how bounded wildcards recover the flexibility erasure takes away

sections.title: Before Generics, Every Collection Was a Bug Waiting to Happen
sections.content:
Before Java 5, collections stored `Object`. You put a `String` in, you got an `Object` out, and you wrote a cast:

```java
List names = new ArrayList();
names.add("Alice");
String first = (String) names.get(0); // manual cast everywhere
```

The compiler had no idea what type was in the list. If a caller accidentally added an `Integer`, you'd find out at runtime via `ClassCastException` — potentially in a completely different part of the codebase from where the bug was introduced. Production debugging nightmare.

**Generics (Java 5, 2004)** moved the type check to **compile time**. You declare `List<String>` and the compiler refuses any non-`String` insertion. The cast on retrieval is inserted by the compiler automatically. At the source level, the code is shorter and safer. At the bytecode level — and this matters for interviews — the generic type parameters are **erased**, replaced with `Object` (or their bounds). The runtime has no idea whether it's holding a `List<String>` or a `List<Integer>`.

This design choice was about **backward compatibility**: Java 5 bytecode had to still run on JVMs that knew nothing about generics, and pre-generics collections code had to keep compiling. C# made the opposite choice (reified generics) and broke backward compatibility to get richer runtime reflection. Java kept the old bytecode shape and paid the price in runtime limitations.

sections.title: What Generics Actually Give You — The Three Benefits
sections.content:
**1. Compile-time type safety.** The compiler catches type mismatches at the source level.
```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Alice");        // OK
names.add(42);             // compile error — before runtime
```

**2. No manual casts.** The compiler inserts casts automatically.
```java
String first = names.get(0); // no (String) cast needed
```
Bytecode-wise, there's still a `checkcast` instruction inserted by the compiler. At source level, the code is clean.

**3. Reusable algorithms and data structures.** You write one `class Stack<T>` and use it for `Stack<Integer>`, `Stack<User>`, `Stack<String>` — with full type safety for each. Before generics, you wrote `Stack` of `Object` and every caller cast manually.

sections.title: The Cost — Type Erasure and What You Lose at Runtime
sections.content:
The compiler enforces generic types, inserts casts, and then **erases** the type parameters in bytecode. Consequences:

**No `new T()`.** The JVM can't know what `T` is at runtime. Workaround: pass a `Class<T>` and use reflection.
```java
<T> T create(Class<T> clazz) throws Exception {
    return clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
}
```

**No `new T[]`.** Same reason. Workaround: `Array.newInstance(clazz, size)` + cast.

**No `instanceof List<String>`.** At runtime it's just `List`. You can write `x instanceof List<?>` (the raw form) but not with a type argument.

**One `Class` object for all parameterizations.** `new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass()` returns **true**. They're the same class at runtime.

**Can't overload by generic type alone.** `void process(List<String>)` and `void process(List<Integer>)` both erase to `process(List)` — compile error.

**Invariance.** `List<Integer>` is **not** a subtype of `List<Number>`, even though `Integer extends Number`. This is what wildcards (`? extends Number`) were created to solve.

sections.title: The Pre-Generics Mess
Generics Fix It at Compile Time
Java's Erasure vs C#'s Reification — Why Java Made This Choice
sections.content:
**Java's erasure model:**
- Pro: old bytecode runs on new JVMs unchanged; pre-generics `List` and post-generics `List<T>` are the same class.
- Pro: smaller runtime, no per-parameterization class objects.
- Con: `new T()`, `new T[]`, `instanceof T` all impossible at runtime.
- Con: bridge methods, unchecked warnings, the wildcard system all exist to work around erasure.

**C#'s reified generics:**
- Pro: `typeof(T)`, `new T()`, `T[]` all work naturally; full runtime reflection over type parameters.
- Pro: `List<int>` is a different type from `List<string>` at runtime — richer type information.
- Con: broke backward compatibility — C# 1.0 code doesn't run unchanged on C# 2.0+ runtime.
- Con: more complex JIT; each parameterization is effectively a distinct type.

**The Java result**: you trade runtime reflection richness for migration pain being near-zero. For an enterprise language where existing codebases must keep compiling and running, this was the right trade in 2004. For Java today, Project Valhalla is exploring ways to add reified primitives and value types — potentially reducing some erasure pain without breaking backward compatibility.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Generics move type checks from runtime to compile time** — no more surprise `ClassCastException`.
- **The compiler inserts casts automatically** — cleaner source, identical bytecode behavior.
- **Type erasure is the cost of backward compatibility** — all parameterizations share the same `Class` at runtime.
- **Can't do `new T()`, `new T[]`, or `instanceof T<...>`** — the type parameter doesn't exist at runtime.
- **`List<Integer>` is not a subtype of `List<Number>`** — invariance; wildcards (`? extends`, `? super`) recover flexibility.
- **C# chose reification and backward incompatibility**; Java chose erasure and compatibility — different languages, different trade-offs.
- **Java 7 diamond operator** (`new ArrayList<>()`) removed most of the verbosity; Java 10+ `var` removes more.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Before generics, collections stored `Object` and you cast on every retrieval — type mismatches only showed up at runtime as `ClassCastException`, often far from the actual bug. Generics moved that check to compile time.

**What generics give you**
- Compile-time type safety: `List<String>.add(42)` is a compile error, not a runtime one
- Automatic cast insertion: you write `String s = list.get(0)`, compiler inserts the cast
- Reusable algorithms and data structures: one `Stack<T>` serves every element type with full safety

**The cost — type erasure**
- `T` is erased to `Object` (or its bound) in bytecode for backward compatibility with pre-generics JVMs
- At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same `Class` — `getClass()` returns the same object
- Consequences: no `new T()`, no `new T[]`, no `instanceof List<String>`, no overload by type parameter alone
- The workarounds use `Class<T>` tokens, reflection, and wildcards

**Invariance and wildcards**
- `List<Integer>` is NOT a subtype of `List<Number>` — the compiler refuses to treat them as interchangeable
- Wildcards (`List<? extends Number>` and `List<? super Integer>`) restore the flexibility erasure takes away
- PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super — is the rule of thumb for choosing

**Java vs C#**
- C# chose reified generics and broke backward compatibility — richer runtime reflection, but old code didn't run unchanged
- Java chose erasure and kept backward compatibility — weaker runtime reflection, but migration pain was near-zero

**Recommendation:** Use generics everywhere you'd otherwise need `Object` + casts — collections, DAOs, service interfaces, utility methods. Lean on **bounded wildcards** (`? extends T`, `? super T`) at API boundaries to keep callers flexible, and use `Class<T>` tokens to work around the runtime limitations when you need them.

sections.title: Why List<String> and List<Integer> Are the Same Class at Runtime
sections.content:
Most developers think of generics as "compile-time type checking for collections." That's correct but incomplete — the interesting part is what happens *after* compilation, and why that limitation shapes how you design APIs.

Before Java 5, collections stored `Object`. You put a `String` in, you got an `Object` out, and you cast it. If someone put an `Integer` into your `List`, you wouldn't know until a `ClassCastException` at runtime — potentially far from the insertion point. **Generics** moved this error to compile time: `List<String>` refuses to accept an `Integer` at the point of insertion, not at the point of retrieval.

The tradeoff Java made to achieve this without breaking existing bytecode is **type erasure**. The compiler verifies all generic types, inserts the necessary casts, and then *erases* the type parameters from the bytecode. At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `List`. They share the same `Class` object — `new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass()` is `true`.

This erasure has concrete consequences that trip up experienced developers: you can't do `instanceof List<String>`, you can't create `new T[]`, and you can't call `T.class`. Understanding *why* these limitations exist — not just memorizing them — is what the interviewer is evaluating.

sections.title: What the Compiler Does: Type Checking, Cast Insertion, and Erasure
sections.content:
The compiler performs three operations with generics, and all three happen before a single line of bytecode is generated.

First, **type checking**. When you write `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()`, the compiler enforces that only `String` values can be added. `names.add(42)` is a compile error — no runtime check needed.

Second, **cast insertion**. When you write `String name = names.get(0)`, the compiler inserts a `(String)` cast into the bytecode. You don't see it in source code, but the bytecode literally contains `checkcast java/lang/String`. Before generics, you wrote this cast yourself — generics just made the compiler do it for you.

Third, **erasure**. The compiler replaces all type parameters with their bounds. `List<String>` becomes `List` (bound is `Object`). `Comparable<T>` becomes `Comparable`. A bounded type like `<T extends Number>` erases to `Number`, not `Object` — this is why bounded generics preserve more type information in the bytecode than unbounded ones.

After these three steps, the resulting bytecode is identical to what you'd write without generics — just with the casts guaranteed to be safe by the compiler's type analysis.

sections.title: The Five Things Erasure Prevents — and the Workarounds That Exist
sections.content:
Type erasure creates specific limitations that every Java developer encounters eventually. Knowing the workaround for each one is what separates a textbook answer from a practical one.

**No `instanceof` on generic types.** You can't write `if (list instanceof List<String>)` because `List<String>` doesn't exist at runtime — it's just `List`. The workaround is checking the element type: store a `Class<T>` token and use `clazz.isInstance(element)`.

**No `new T()` or `new T[]`.** The JVM doesn't know what `T` is at runtime, so it can't allocate the right type. The workaround is passing a `Class<T>` parameter — the factory pattern: `T instance = clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`.

**No generic exceptions.** You can't write `catch (MyException<T>)` because the JVM's exception handling works on erased types. This is rarely a problem in practice but occasionally surprises framework developers.

**Bridge methods in inheritance.** When a generic class is subclassed with a concrete type, the compiler generates **bridge methods** to maintain polymorphism. A class implementing `Comparable<MyClass>` gets both `compareTo(MyClass)` and a synthetic `compareTo(Object)` that casts and delegates. These show up in reflection with `isBridge() == true`.

**No overloading by type parameter alone.** `void process(List<String> s)` and `void process(List<Integer> i)` have the same erasure — `process(List)` — so they can't coexist in the same class.

sections.title: Bounded Wildcards: The API Design Tool Most Developers Underuse
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Generics = compile-time type safety** — `List<String>` won't accept `Integer`; the compiler inserts casts automatically.
- **Type erasure: all generic types become raw `List` in bytecode** — no `instanceof List<String>` or `new T[]` at runtime.
- **Bounded types erase to their bound** — `<T extends Number>` becomes `Number` in bytecode, not `Object`.
- **Bridge methods preserve polymorphism** — compiler generates synthetic methods when a generic class is subclassed with a concrete type.
- **PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super** — `List<? extends Number>` for reading; `List<? super Integer>` for writing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Generics give you compile-time type safety — `List<String>` won't accept an `Integer` and the compiler inserts casts for you. The tradeoff is **type erasure**: after compilation, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `List`.

**Consequences of erasure:**
- No `instanceof List<String>` — the type parameter doesn't exist at runtime
- No `new T[]` or `new T()` — the JVM doesn't know what `T` is at runtime
- Workaround: pass a `Class<T>` token and use `Array.newInstance(clazz, length)` or reflection

**What survives erasure:**
- Bounded types erase to their bound: `<T extends Number>` becomes `Number` in bytecode, not `Object`
- Bridge methods are generated when a generic class is subclassed with a concrete type, maintaining polymorphism

**Wildcards (PECS):**
- `List<? extends Number>` accepts `List<Integer>` or `List<Double>` — for reading (Producer Extends)
- `List<? super Integer>` accepts `List<Number>` or `List<Object>` — for writing (Consumer Super)
- Generic collections are invariant without wildcards: `List<Integer>` is NOT a `List<Number>`

I recommend following PECS for any generic API that accepts or returns collections.

questions.question: What are `?`, `? extends T`, and `? super T` in Java generics — when do you use each?
questions.title: Bounded vs Unbounded Wildcards in Java — `?`, `? extends T`, `? super T` with Real Examples
questions.direct_answer: **`?` (unbounded)** = "some unknown type" — you can read as `Object` and can't add anything except `null`. **`? extends T` (upper-bounded)** = "T or any subtype" — safe to **read** as `T`, can't **add** (compiler doesn't know the exact subtype). **`? super T` (lower-bounded)** = "T or any supertype" — safe to **add** `T` or any subtype of `T`, reads come back as `Object`. **When to use**: `? extends` for reading (producer), `? super` for writing (consumer), `?` when you don't care about the type at all (e.g., counting elements). The mnemonic is **PECS** — Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the read-only and write-only nature of each wildcard form and can apply PECS to real API design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing `? extends T` as writable (it isn't — except for null). Thinking `? super T` reads as T (it reads as Object). Using raw `List` instead of `List<?>`
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why `? extends` is read-only via the compiler's capture mechanism. Use `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` as the canonical PECS example and explain why both bounds are needed

sections.title: Wildcards Exist Because `List<Integer>` Is Not a `List<Number>`
sections.content:
Generics are **invariant**: `List<Integer>` is **not** a subtype of `List<Number>`, even though `Integer` is a subtype of `Number`. This is a consequence of type safety — if it were allowed, you could do this:

```java
List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>();
List<Number> nums = ints; // imagine this were legal
nums.add(3.14); // adds a Double to what's supposed to be List<Integer>
Integer bad = ints.get(0); // ClassCastException at runtime
```

Invariance prevents that. But it's inconvenient: a method that should accept "any list of numbers" can't just declare `List<Number>`. That's where **wildcards** come in — they restore controlled flexibility without breaking type safety.

There are three wildcard forms:
- **`?`** — "some unknown type." Fully generic, read-only (except for `null`).
- **`? extends T`** — "T or any subtype of T." Upper-bounded; safe to read as T, can't add.
- **`? super T`** — "T or any supertype of T." Lower-bounded; safe to add T or subtypes, reads come back as Object.

The rule of thumb for choosing is **PECS**: use `extends` when the collection **produces** values (you read from it), use `super` when the collection **consumes** values (you write to it).

sections.title: `?`, `? extends T`, `? super T` Side by Side
sections.content:
| Form | Meaning | Safe to READ | Safe to ADD | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `List<?>` | Any type (unknown) | Yes — as `Object` | Only `null` | Size queries, element printing, "I don't care about the type" |
| `List<? extends Number>` | `Number` or any subtype | Yes — as `Number` | Only `null` | Reading from a collection (producer) |
| `List<? super Integer>` | `Integer` or any supertype | Yes — as `Object` | `Integer` or any subtype of `Integer` | Writing into a collection (consumer) |
| `List<Number>` (no wildcard) | Exactly `Number` (invariant) | Yes — as `Number` | `Number` or any subtype | Generic code that both reads and writes |

Notice the fundamental asymmetry: `? extends` lets you **read** a known type but not add; `? super` lets you **add** a known type but not read it precisely.

sections.title: `? extends T` — For Reading (Producer)
`? super T` — For Writing (Consumer)
The Canonical PECS Example — `Collections.copy`
`?` (Unbounded) — When Type Doesn't Matter
Wildcards vs Named Type Parameters — When to Choose Which
sections.content:
**Use wildcards when**:
- The method only uses the parameter at one position.
- You don't need to relate multiple parameters to the same type.
- You want the flexibility of accepting subtypes or supertypes.

**Use named type parameters `<T>` when**:
- Two parameters must share the same type: `<T> void swap(List<T> list, int i, int j)`.
- The return type depends on an argument: `<T> T first(List<T> list)`.
- You need to reference the type inside the method body (`T.class` via a Class<T> parameter, for instance).

**Convention**:
- API boundaries → prefer wildcards for **input** parameters (maximizes caller flexibility).
- Return types → avoid wildcards; they force callers to use wildcard-typed variables everywhere.
- Internal methods → named type parameters are usually clearer.

**The common mistake**: using raw `List` instead of `List<?>`. Raw types disable all generic checks; `List<?>` is safely read-only with clear compiler guarantees.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Invariance forces wildcards to exist** — `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`.
- **`? extends T`**: read-only as T. Producer. Can't add except `null`.
- **`? super T`**: write-friendly for T and subtypes. Consumer. Reads back as `Object`.
- **`?`**: unbounded; read-only as `Object`; use when type doesn't matter.
- **PECS**: Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super.
- **`Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)`** is the JDK's canonical PECS example.
- **Prefer wildcards at API inputs** for caller flexibility; **avoid them in return types**.
- **Use `<T>` when you need to relate multiple parameters or a return value to the same type.**

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Wildcards exist because Java generics are **invariant** — `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`. That's safe but inflexible, and wildcards restore controlled flexibility.

**Three wildcard forms**
- **`?`** — some unknown type; read-only as `Object`; use when the type doesn't matter (e.g., `printAll(List<?>)`, `size()`)
- **`? extends T`** — T or any subtype; safe to read as T; can't add (compiler doesn't know the exact subtype)
- **`? super T`** — T or any supertype; safe to add T and its subtypes; reads come back as `Object`

**The mnemonic: PECS**
- **Producer-Extends** — if you're reading from the collection, use `? extends T`
- **Consumer-Super** — if you're writing into the collection, use `? super T`

**Why the asymmetry**
- `? extends T`: the list might be `List<Integer>` or `List<Double>` — adding anything risks mismatching the actual type
- `? super T`: the list is guaranteed to accept T and its subtypes, so adding is safe; but reads can only guarantee `Object`

**Canonical example — `Collections.copy`**
- `copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` — source is a producer, destination is a consumer
- Lets you copy from `List<Integer>` into `List<Number>` without losing type safety

**When to use named type parameters instead**
- Two parameters must share the same type: `<T> void swap(List<T>, int, int)`
- Return type depends on an argument
- You need to reference the type inside the method

**Recommendation:** For API inputs, prefer wildcards — they maximize caller flexibility. `? extends T` when you only read, `? super T` when you only write, `?` when you don't care. Reserve named type parameters `<T>` for when you must relate multiple parameters or a return value to the same type. And never use raw `List` when `List<?>` is available — raw types disable all generic type checking.

questions.direct_answer: **PECS** — **Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super** — is Joshua Bloch's rule for picking the right wildcard. If the parameter **produces** values your method reads, declare it `? extends T`. If the parameter **consumes** values your method writes, declare it `? super T`. If it does **both** (reads and writes T), don't use wildcards — use a named type parameter `<T>`. **Canonical example**: `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` — source produces T, destination consumes T. The same rule applies to streams (`Stream.forEach(Consumer<? super T>)`), comparators (`Comparator<? super T>`), and any method that reads from or writes to a collection.

sections.title: One Rule Most Wildcard Decisions Collapse Into
sections.content:
Joshua Bloch's *Effective Java* item on wildcards gives a one-line rule: **PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super**. It's the decision procedure for almost every wildcard you'll ever write.

The intuition: a generic parameter is either **producing** values for your method to consume, or **consuming** values your method produces, or both. If it's only producing, the parameter is a read-only source — use `? extends T` so callers can pass any subtype of T. If it's only consuming, the parameter is a write-only sink — use `? super T` so callers can pass any supertype. If it does both, wildcards can't express the relationship cleanly, so use a named type parameter `<T>`.

The JDK's own API follows PECS almost perfectly once you start looking. `Stream.forEach(Consumer<? super T>)`, `Collections.sort(List<T>, Comparator<? super T>)`, `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` — all apply the same rule. Once you see it, API design becomes mechanical.

sections.title: The Three Cases — Producer, Consumer, Both
`Collections.copy` — The Canonical PECS Signature
PECS in the JDK — Where You'll Encounter It Every Day
sections.content:
**`Stream.forEach(Consumer<? super T>)`** — the consumer is a sink you pass T values to. A `Consumer<Object>` can accept `T` (since T is a subtype of Object), so `? super T` lets callers pass `Consumer<Object>` when they have one, not just `Consumer<T>`.

**`Comparator.thenComparing(Comparator<? super T>)`** — comparators of a supertype work on T (you can compare `User` objects with a `Comparator<Object>` based on identity). `? super T` accepts them.

**`Collections.sort(List<T>, Comparator<? super T>)`** — same reason. The list is `List<T>` because sort reads and writes; the comparator is `? super T` because it only consumes T.

**`Function<? super T, ? extends R>` in `Stream.map`** — both bounds. The function consumes T (so `? super T` accepts supertype functions) and produces R (so `? extends R` accepts subtype-returning functions). This is the most precise form and the one you'll see all over the streams API.

Once you notice the pattern, every wildcard in the JDK tells you exactly what role the parameter plays — you don't have to read the implementation to know whether a value is being read or written.

sections.title: When NOT to Apply PECS — And Common Pitfalls
Key Points
sections.content:
- **PECS** = **Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super**.
- **Producer (you read from it)** → `? extends T`.
- **Consumer (you write to it)** → `? super T`.
- **Both** → named type parameter `<T>`.
- **`Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)`** is the JDK's canonical example.
- **PECS applies to parameters, not return types** — wildcard return types pollute caller code.
- **Streams use it everywhere**: `Stream.map(Function<? super T, ? extends R>)`, `Stream.forEach(Consumer<? super T>)`.
- **When in doubt, ask: does my method read from this, write to it, or both?** The answer chooses the wildcard.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
PECS is the one rule that collapses most wildcard decisions into a simple question: "does my method read from this parameter, write to it, or both?"

**The rule**
- **P**roducer **E**xtends — if the parameter is a source you read from, use `? extends T`
- **C**onsumer **S**uper — if the parameter is a sink you write to, use `? super T`
- If the parameter does both, don't use wildcards — use a named type parameter `<T>`

**Canonical example — `Collections.copy`**
- `copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)`
- Source is a producer of T — you only read from it — so `? extends T`
- Destination is a consumer of T — you only write to it — so `? super T`
- This lets you call `copy(List<Object>, List<Integer>)` — source is a subtype, destination is a supertype

**Why it works**
- `? extends T`: any subtype fits; safe to read as T; can't add because the compiler doesn't know the exact subtype
- `? super T`: any supertype fits; safe to add T and subtypes; reads come back as Object because we only know it's at least T
- Named `<T>`: when you need to both read and write T, wildcards can't express that it's the same T

**PECS is everywhere in the JDK**
- `Stream.forEach(Consumer<? super T>)` — consumer accepts T, so supertype consumers work
- `Collections.sort(List<T>, Comparator<? super T>)` — comparator only consumes T
- `Stream.map(Function<? super T, ? extends R>)` — function consumes T (super T), produces R (extends R)

**When NOT to use wildcards**
- Return types — they force every caller to use wildcard types
- Two parameters that must share the same type — wildcards lose the relationship

**Recommendation:** Memorize PECS and the 'get and put' mental model — they'll carry you through 95% of API design decisions. Use `? extends T` for inputs you only read, `? super T` for inputs you only write, and a named `<T>` when you need both. Don't wildcard return types, and never fall back to raw types.

questions.question: Why is `new T[]` illegal in Java? Explain reifiable vs non-reifiable types and the workarounds.
questions.title: Why You Can't Create a Generic Array in Java — Reifiable vs Non-Reifiable Types
questions.direct_answer: **`new T[]` is illegal** because Java arrays are **reified** (store their element type at runtime and do a runtime type check on every write) while generics are **erased** (no runtime type info). If the compiler allowed `new T[]`, the array would at runtime be a plain `Object[]` that wouldn't enforce the `T` constraint — you'd get silent corruption until a `ClassCastException` on retrieval. **Reifiable types** (primitives, `Object`, raw types, `?`-unbounded wildcards) have complete runtime type info. **Non-reifiable types** (`T`, `List<String>`, `List<? extends Number>`) don't. **Workarounds**: declare as `Object[]` with a cast plus `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")`, or pass a `Class<T>` and use `Array.newInstance(clazz, size)`.

sections.title: Arrays and Generics Live in Two Incompatible Worlds
sections.content:
Java has two ways of expressing "a container of elements with a known type": **arrays** and **generics**. They look similar in source code — `String[]` and `List<String>` — but under the hood, the JVM treats them completely differently. Arrays are **reified**: the JVM knows at runtime that a `String[]` stores strings and refuses any attempt to store a non-String (`ArrayStoreException`). Generics are **erased**: at runtime, `List<String>` is just `List`; the JVM has no idea what it's supposed to contain.

On top of that, arrays are **covariant** (`String[]` is a subtype of `Object[]`) while generics are **invariant** (`List<String>` is NOT a subtype of `List<Object>`). Covariance + erasure would be catastrophic. If `new T[]` compiled, the JVM would create an `Object[]` at runtime with no `T` check — and since arrays are covariant, you could assign it to `Object[]` and stuff any type into it. The `T` promise becomes a lie.

Java's designers closed the loophole by making generic array creation a **compile-time error**. This forces you to think about the unsafety and adopt one of the explicit workarounds — `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` with an `Object[]` cast, or runtime reflection via `Array.newInstance(clazz, size)`.

sections.title: Reifiable vs Non-Reifiable Types — The Distinction That Determines What You Can Put in an Array
sections.content:
The JLS classifies types as **reifiable** (complete runtime type info available) or **non-reifiable** (type info partially or fully erased).

**Reifiable types — safe for array creation:**
- Primitives: `int[]`, `double[]`
- Non-generic reference types: `String[]`, `User[]`
- Raw types: `List[]` (without a type parameter)
- Unbounded wildcard parameterizations: `List<?>[]`
- Arrays of reifiable types: `String[][]`

**Non-reifiable types — `new` is a compile error:**
- Type parameters: `new T[10]` — ILLEGAL
- Parameterized types with arguments: `new List<String>[10]` — ILLEGAL
- Bounded wildcards: `new List<? extends Number>[10]` — ILLEGAL

The rule: **if the type's full information survives to runtime, you can create an array of it. Otherwise, you can't.** Raw `List[]` is reifiable because raw `List` has no type parameter to erase. `List<?>[]` is reifiable because `?` is "any type" — no specific information to erase.

sections.title: What Would Break If `new T[]` Were Legal
sections.content:
Imagine Java allowed it. Here's the corruption:

```java
<T> T[] create() {
    return new T[10]; // hypothetically legal
}

String[] strings = this.<String>create(); // runtime: just an Object[]
Object[] objects = strings;               // arrays are covariant, so OK
objects[0] = 42;                          // no array store check? silent corruption
String s = strings[0];                    // ClassCastException or worse: silent wrong type
```

Arrays normally protect themselves with `ArrayStoreException` — `Object[] arr = new String[10]; arr[0] = 42;` throws at the assignment because the array knows it's a `String[]`. But a hypothetical `new T[]` would be a bare `Object[]` at runtime with no `String` memory — the assignment would succeed, the retrieval would either cast or silently return the wrong type. Generic type safety collapses entirely.

This is precisely why the compiler rejects `new T[]`.

sections.title: The Two Real-World Workarounds
The Varargs Trap — Why Generic Varargs Got `@SafeVarargs`
sections.content:
Varargs secretly create an array. When you write:
```java
public <T> void process(T... items) { ... }
process("a", "b", "c"); // compiler creates new String[]{"a","b","c"}
```
The compiler creates a `T[]` array under the hood — which means varargs with generic parameters hit the same non-reifiable problem. The compiler warns about "possible heap pollution":
```java
List<String>[] lists = new List[] { Arrays.asList("a"), Arrays.asList("b") }; // raw List[] + unchecked
Object[] objs = lists; // covariance
objs[0] = Arrays.asList(1, 2); // an Integer list went into a List<String>[]!
String s = lists[0].get(0); // ClassCastException deep in user code
```

Java 7 added **`@SafeVarargs`** for methods the author has verified don't leak the varargs array. It suppresses the warning on the call site. Library methods like `Arrays.asList` and `List.of` are marked `@SafeVarargs` because they don't store the array long-term; they copy from it and throw it away.

sections.title: When Generic Arrays Matter and When You Don't Care
sections.content:
**When it actually matters**
- Writing low-level collection classes (your own `Stack<T>`, `Queue<T>`, custom buffer).
- Implementing libraries where callers pass in varargs with generic types.
- Reflecting on method signatures that return `T[]`.

**When you don't care**
- Application code. Use `ArrayList<T>` or any `List<T>` — the API is identical to an array for iteration, indexing is `get(i)`/`set(i,v)`, and the JIT compiles the operations down to nearly-identical machine code. The only reason to pick a raw array is performance-critical primitive-valued hot loops (`int[]` is faster than `List<Integer>` because of boxing).

**When to use `Array.newInstance` vs `Object[]` cast**
- `Array.newInstance` when you need to **return** the array to callers — true runtime type, ArrayStoreException protection.
- `Object[]` + cast for **private, internal** storage that never leaves the class. Simpler, no need to keep a Class token around.

**Avoid entirely**: methods that accept and return `T[]` — they force callers to deal with the non-reifiable problem. Return `List<T>` instead, let callers convert to array with `list.toArray(new T[0])` if they need it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Arrays are reified** (runtime type info + covariant) — they throw `ArrayStoreException` for wrong inserts.
- **Generics are erased** (no runtime type info + invariant) — they rely on the compiler for safety.
- **`new T[]` is illegal** because combining erased types with covariant arrays would silently break type safety.
- **Reifiable types**: primitives, non-generic types, raw types, unbounded wildcards — arrays of these are legal.
- **Non-reifiable types**: `T`, `List<String>`, `List<? extends Number>` — arrays of these are compile errors.
- **Workarounds**: `(T[]) new Object[n]` for internal storage; `Array.newInstance(clazz, n)` for returnable arrays; just use `List<T>`.
- **Varargs silently create arrays** — generic varargs need `@SafeVarargs` when the author guarantees no heap pollution.
- **In application code**: prefer `ArrayList<T>` over any generic-array workaround.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Arrays and generics live in two incompatible worlds. Arrays are reified and covariant — they know their element type at runtime and `String[]` is a subtype of `Object[]`. Generics are erased and invariant — at runtime `List<String>` is just `List`, and `List<String>` is NOT a subtype of `List<Object>`.

**Why `new T[]` is banned**
- If allowed, the array would at runtime be a bare `Object[]` — no `T` enforcement
- Because arrays are covariant, you could assign it to `Object[]` and store anything in it
- The generic type safety would silently collapse; you'd get `ClassCastException` or wrong values on retrieval
- Java closes this loophole at compile time instead

**Reifiable vs non-reifiable types**
- Reifiable: primitives, non-generic types, raw types, unbounded wildcards — arrays of these are legal
- Non-reifiable: `T`, `List<String>`, `List<? extends Number>` — arrays of these are compile errors
- Rule: if the full type information survives erasure, arrays work; otherwise they don't

**Workarounds**
- Internal storage: `(T[]) new Object[n]` with `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` — fine as long as the array doesn't leak out of the class
- Returnable array: `Array.newInstance(clazz, n)` — creates a real `String[]` at runtime using the Class token
- Best option in application code: just use `ArrayList<T>`

**The varargs trap**
- Varargs secretly create an array: `T... items` becomes `T[] items` in bytecode
- Same non-reifiability issue; compiler warns about "heap pollution"
- `@SafeVarargs` (Java 7) suppresses the warning when the method author guarantees no unsafe use

**Recommendation:** In application code, use `List<T>` or `ArrayList<T>` — you almost never need a generic array. For library code where you must expose arrays, use `Array.newInstance(clazz, size)` with a `Class<T>` token — it produces a true runtime-typed array with `ArrayStoreException` protection. Reserve the `(T[]) new Object[n]` trick for private internal storage that never escapes the class.
